metadata.narrative: I'm a tech lead for a 12-person remote team maintaining a fairly old payments service. Our pull requests have become huge, reviews take days, and people complain that reviews are either rubber-stamps or endless arguments about style. We already have CI and linters, but bugs and hard-to-change code still slip through. Should we redesign our code review process, and if so what rules should we adopt around PR size, reviewer expectations, security checks, response times, automation, and review culture? What tradeoffs should I expect if we push for smaller, faster reviews without lowering quality?
metadata.run_desc: aus_agent research harness (bedrock/au.anthropic.claude-sonnet-5): continuous single-agent full-text search with sparse committed context and line-per-sentence cited prose answers parsed into the organizer schema.

answer.text: Yes, you should redesign the process, because the symptoms you describe — huge PRs, multi-day reviews, and reviews that swing between rubber-stamping and style arguments — are well-documented failure modes with concrete, evidence-backed fixes.

Start with PR size, since size is the single biggest lever on review quality: a Cisco Systems study analyzed by SmartBear found reviewers caught defects effectively only up to about 400 lines of code, after which detection ability dropped sharply, and a Shopify study by Kononenko et al. found developers strongly preferred small, single-purpose PRs, with review effectiveness degrading as size grew.

A separate analysis across real PR histories found an even tighter sweet spot of roughly 25-100 lines, with about 50 as ideal: 50-line PRs merged about 40% faster than 250-line PRs, were 15% less likely to be reverted, and drew 40% more review comments per line.
Adopt a soft limit near 300-400 lines of diff as a warning threshold, and use stacked/sequential PRs to break large features into reviewable slices.

On reviewer expectations, adopt a documented priority order modeled on Google's engineering practices: design first, then functionality and edge cases, then complexity, then tests, then style and documentation last.

Forbid blocking a PR on personal style preference, require the word "Nit" to prefix purely stylistic comments so authors know they're non-blocking, and define narrow emergency criteria — outage, production security hole, legal issue — as the only valid reasons to skip normal rigor.
Reviewers should also call out good decisions, not just problems, since positive reinforcement improves the review relationship.
On response times, set an explicit internal SLA rather than leaving it implicit, since unclear response norms are a known source of remote-worker anxiety and slowed feedback loops.

A concrete, tested rule is returning an initial review within one business day, since slower turnaround creates a vicious cycle: waiting developers context-switch away, PRs grow larger while waiting, and pressure to "just merge it" degrades code health.

Your SLA should be written down, easy to find, define what counts as urgent versus routine, include an escalation path, and be periodically measured so unmet targets flag understaffing rather than being silently tolerated.

On automation, keep leaning on CI and linters but recognize their blind spots: static analysis cannot reliably catch authentication/authorization misconfiguration, weak cryptography choices, insecure database connection settings, or compromised third-party dependencies, which explains why bugs still slip through despite existing tooling.

Layer in dedicated SAST tools (SonarQube, Veracode, Snyk Code are cited examples) for injection and buffer-overflow patterns, plus software composition analysis tools like Dependabot or Snyk Open Source for vulnerable dependencies, freeing human reviewers to focus on design and business logic.

A real-world case at the company Stim showed the payoff: after introducing tooling and quality gates requiring 80% coverage on new code, average coverage across 70 repositories rose from about 20% to over 60% within nine months, and one legacy application surfaced 55,000 flagged critical issues including SQL injection risks.
Security checks deserve explicit treatment given this is a payments service.

A secure code review should systematically examine seven mechanisms — authentication, authorization, session management, data validation, error handling, logging, and encryption — a structure formalized in defense-sector application security guidance.

If your service touches cardholder data, PCI DSS 4.0 Requirement 6 is directly applicable: it mandates independent code review before release, approved by someone other than the author, annual secure-coding training for developers, explicit mitigation of injection, overflow, and authentication attacks, and critical security patches installed within one month of release.
Bake a short security checklist derived from these two sources into your PR template so it isn't left to reviewer memory.

On review culture, treat bikeshedding as a symptom rather than pure noise: one analysis frames style disputes through accommodation theory, arguing developers fight over indentation or semicolons because divergence feels like a social signal of disrespect rather than because the technical stakes are high, and that discussing each person's coding background can defuse conflict faster than rules alone.

Practical habits help too: address the code rather than the author ("what is this log for?" instead of "why did you do this?"), phrase suggestions rather than commands, and cultivate a blameless, safe-to-fail culture where mistakes become lessons rather than grounds for punishment.
For unavoidably large changes, that same guidance recommends a live walkthrough or collective review session rather than relying purely on asynchronous comments.
Now the tradeoffs to expect from pushing toward smaller, faster reviews.

Smaller PRs measurably reduce revert rates up to a point, but going below roughly 25 lines starts increasing revert rates again and lowering total code shipped, so there is a floor as well as a ceiling on size.

Very small batches push toward trunk-based development patterns, which speed bug detection and simplify each review, but introduce more frequent merge conflicts and make rolling back a single problematic change harder to isolate without a dedicated feature branch.
Faster SLAs cost reviewer attention, since a one-business-day norm requires all twelve team members to build review-checking into their daily rhythm rather than batching it whenever convenient.

Resist using "smaller reviews" as an excuse for wholesale rewrites of the legacy service; the better path is incremental refactoring embedded in ordinary feature work, distinguishing prudent-and-deliberate technical debt from reckless messes, and quantifying the cost of bad code to justify investment, since full rewrites are described as "almost always the wrong answer".

Finally, expect an adjustment period: smaller PRs generate more review comments per line changed, which can initially feel like added friction even though it reflects reviewers actually engaging rather than rubber-stamping.

input.system_prompt:
# AUS research agent

You are a research agent for TREC RAG 2026. Produce a complete,
well-organized, evidence-grounded response using only the available
search/retrieval tools and evidence returned by them. Prior knowledge may help
you choose searches, but it is not evidence and must not support factual claims.

## Scope interpretation

Infer the full deliverable from the entire request, including every concrete
requirement, audience constraint, comparison, example, and requested format.
If light framing such as "overview" or "outline" conflicts with substantial
concrete requirements, the concrete requirements define the real scope.
Resolve ambiguity toward the most complete reasonable interpretation that
stays in scope. Do not ask the user clarifying or confirming questions; proceed
on the strongest reasonable reading.

## Internal success plan

Before the first search, determine internally:

1. **End goal** — one sentence describing what a complete deliverable provides.
2. **Concrete minimum requirements** — the checkable floor that must be met
   before the response is shippable.
3. **Target/excellence requirements** — what a notably strong response adds
   beyond the minimum without expanding scope.
4. **Coverage areas** — the independent topics, claims, comparisons, examples,
   dates, people, mechanisms, or perspectives that require evidence.

Use these requirements to plan searches, track coverage gaps, judge evidence,
and decide when to stop. Do not expose this internal plan unless the requested
answer itself calls for it.

## Research workflow

1. Begin with multiple complementary queries in parallel across independent
   coverage areas.
2. Move from broad discovery to targeted follow-ups for specific names, dates,
   mechanisms, examples, definitions, causal claims, and disputed points.
3. Reformulate weak queries instead of accepting poor coverage. Try synonyms,
   alternative terminology, narrower entities, and different phrasings.
4. Actively search for counter-evidence, contradictions, limitations, and
   missing perspectives when they matter to the request.
5. Continually compare gathered evidence against the minimum and target
   requirements. Search the remaining gaps rather than repeating already
   covered claims.
6. Every tool call must have a concrete purpose tied to an unmet requirement
   or evidence gap. Do not call a tool solely to create another model turn. If
   no meaningful gap remains, write the final report in that same turn.

Search results already contain document text. Inspect that text directly; do
not call another tool merely to fetch the same document. The search tool
normally stages at most about 4,096 tokens per result; request a different
`budget_tokens_per_result` only when a query genuinely needs a different
per-document evidence depth.

## Staged and committed evidence

Every retrieval batch is staged for exactly the immediately following model
turn.

- On that turn, `commit_context` must be the first control action.
- List only documents whose full text should persist into later turns.
- Commit at most `6` documents from one staged batch;
  usually commit fewer.
- Every selection reason must identify the document's distinct contribution:
  the specific fact, date, name, mechanism, example, perspective,
  counter-evidence, contradiction, or coverage gap it uniquely supports.
- Never recommit an already committed docid.
- Skip semantically similar documents when they support the same claim.
  Commit both only when each contributes materially different evidence.
- Every staged occurrence not selected is compacted/redacted before the
  following turn. No unresolved staged batch carries forward.
- New search calls may follow `commit_context` in the same turn.

Only committed evidence may support the final response. Track which committed
docids support which claims. If available evidence does not support a requested
point, state the evidence gap rather than inventing an answer.

## Budget and stopping

The research-context budget is 500,000 tokens measured from the current
generation's provider-reported input tokens. That input already represents the
accumulated conversation: system prompt, request, retained history, committed
full-text evidence, and the immediately previous staged tool results. Do not
sum input-token counts from multiple generations; that would count the same
retained context repeatedly.

The budget is a hard ceiling, not a spending target. Unused budget creates no
obligation to continue researching. After satisfying the concrete minimum,
improve toward the target/excellence requirements only when you can identify a
specific weakness whose resolution would materially improve the answer.

Stop researching when any of these is true:

1. the target/excellence requirements are met;
2. the current generation input context budget is exhausted; or
3. further searches are unlikely to produce meaningful improvement.

If stopping before all desired coverage is supported, produce the best answer
the committed evidence permits and explicitly identify the remaining evidence
gaps.

## Final response contract

When research is complete, emit no tool calls and write the final report as
plain flowing prose in that same turn:

- Write exactly one sentence per line, in reading order. Blank lines between
  thematic groups are allowed.
- Cite evidence by placing committed docids in square-bracket markers at the
  end of the supporting sentence's line, e.g.
  `Vaccination reduced hospitalizations among older adults. [docid_1] [docid_2]`
- Citation markers are stripped from the submitted sentence, so a marker must
  never act as a word in the sentence: write `the trial reports X [docid].`,
  never `as [docid] reports, X.`
- Cite at most three docids per sentence, and only docids that directly
  support that sentence. Every factual sentence should carry at least one
  citation. Use only committed docids; never fabricate facts or identifiers.
- Organize the report through sentence order and clear topic sentences. Do not
  use Markdown syntax (headings, bullets, numbering, bold, fences), JSON, or
  any preamble, meta-commentary, or closing remarks around the report; every
  line must be a report sentence.
- Aim for about 950 words, excluding citation markers. 1024 words is a hard
  limit set by the evaluation, and an over-length report costs a full rewrite,
  so plan the report's scope to land under the target rather than writing long
  and trimming.
- If validation feedback identifies problems (uncommitted docids, Markdown or
  JSON formatting, excessive citations, missing citations, or excessive
  length), correct the report on the next turn in this same continuous
  conversation using this same contract.
- There is no separate finalizer, formatter, or compression phase.

Yes, you should redesign the process, because the symptoms you describe — huge PRs, multi-day reviews, and reviews that swing between rubber-stamping and style arguments — are well-documented failure modes with concrete, evidence-backed fixes rather than random bad luck.

Start with PR size, since size is the single biggest lever on review quality: a Cisco Systems study analyzed by SmartBear found that reviewers caught defects effectively only up to about 400 lines of code, after which detection ability dropped sharply, and a Shopify study by Kononenko et al. found developers strongly preferred small, single-purpose PRs and that review effectiveness degraded as size grew [shard_05415_42728].
A separate data analysis across real PR histories found an even tighter sweet spot: roughly 25-100 lines, with about 50 lines as the ideal, since 50-line PRs merged about 40% faster than 250-line PRs, were 15% less likely to be reverted, and drew 40% more review comments per line [shard_06420_4716].
Given your payments service's age and complexity, adopt a hard-ish soft limit near 300-400 lines of diff as a warning threshold, and treat anything larger as requiring justification or splitting, using stacked/sequential PRs to break large features into reviewable slices [shard_05415_42728].

On reviewer expectations, adopt a documented priority order for what reviewers look at, modeled on Google's engineering practices: design first, then functionality and edge cases, then complexity, then tests, then style and documentation last [shard_00995_28862].
Explicitly forbid blocking a PR on personal style preference, require the word "Nit" to prefix any purely stylistic comment so authors know it's non-blocking, and define narrow emergency criteria (major outage, production security hole, legal issue) as the only valid reasons to skip normal rigor [shard_00995_28862].
Reviewers should also actively call out good decisions, not just problems, since positive reinforcement improves the review relationship over time [shard_00995_28862].

On response times, set an explicit internal SLA rather than leaving it implicit, because unclear response norms are a known source of remote-worker anxiety and slowed feedback loops [shard_05948_11582].
A concrete, tested rule is returning an initial review within one business day, since slower turnaround creates a vicious cycle: waiting developers context-switch to other work, PRs grow larger while waiting, and pressure to "just merge it" degrades code health [shard_00230_31180].
Your SLA should be written down, easy to find, define what counts as urgent versus routine, include an escalation path, and be periodically measured so unmet targets flag understaffing or overload rather than being silently tolerated [shard_05948_11582].

On automation, keep leaning on CI and linters but recognize their blind spots: static analysis tools cannot reliably catch authentication/authorization misconfiguration, weak cryptography choices, insecure database connection settings, or compromised third-party dependencies, which explains why bugs still slip through despite existing tooling [shard_04995_50083].
Layer in dedicated SAST tools (examples cited include SonarQube, Veracode, and Snyk Code) for injection, buffer overflow, and misconfiguration patterns, plus software composition analysis tools like Dependabot or Snyk Open Source specifically for vulnerable dependencies, since these free human reviewers to focus on design and business logic rather than low-hanging-fruit bugs [shard_01444_2545].
A real-world case at the company Stim showed the payoff of combining automation with process: after introducing tooling and quality gates requiring 80% test coverage on new code, average coverage across 70 repositories rose from about 20% to over 60% within nine months, and a single legacy application surfaced 55,000 flagged critical issues including SQL injection risks [shard_05202_34025].

Security checks deserve explicit, separate treatment given this is a payments service.
A secure code review should systematically examine seven mechanisms: authentication, authorization, session management, data validation, error handling, logging, and encryption, a structure originally formalized in defense-sector application security guidance [shard_00412_34851].
If your service ever touches cardholder data, PCI DSS 4.0's Requirement 6 is directly applicable: it mandates independent code review before release (reviewed by someone other than the author, approved by management), annual secure-coding training for developers, explicit mitigation of injection, buffer/pointer overflow, and authentication/authorization attacks, and installation of critical security patches within one month of release [shard_05960_64676].
Bake a short security checklist derived from these two sources into your PR template so it is not left to reviewer memory.

On review culture, treat bikeshedding as a symptom rather than pure noise: one analysis frames style disputes through accommodation theory, arguing developers fight over indentation or semicolons because divergence feels like a social signal of disrespect, not because the technical stakes are high, and that discussing each person's coding background can defuse the conflict faster than rules alone [shard_03002_40112].
Practical language habits help too: reviewers should address the code rather than the author ("what is this log for?" instead of "why did you do this?"), phrase suggestions rather than commands, and teams should cultivate a blameless, safe-to-fail culture where mistakes are treated as lessons rather than grounds for punishment [shard_02864_78852].
For unavoidably large or complex changes, that same guidance recommends a live walkthrough or collective review session rather than relying purely on asynchronous comments [shard_02864_78852].

Now the tradeoffs you should expect if you push hard toward smaller, faster reviews.
Smaller PRs and faster turnaround measurably increase total shipped code volume and reduce revert rates up to a point, but going below roughly 25 lines per PR starts increasing revert rates again and lowering total code shipped, so there is a floor as well as a ceiling on size [shard_06420_4716].
Adopting very small batches pushes you toward trunk-based development patterns, which speed up bug detection and simplify each individual review, but introduce more frequent merge conflicts and make rolling back a single problematic change harder to isolate since there's no separate feature branch holding prior state [shard_00338_15959].
Faster review SLAs cost reviewer attention and context-switching capacity, since a one-business-day norm requires all 12 team members to build review checking into their daily rhythm rather than reviewers batching it whenever convenient [shard_00230_31180].
On the legacy-code side, resist the urge to use "smaller reviews" as an excuse for wholesale rewrites; the recommended approach is incremental refactoring embedded in ordinary feature work, distinguishing prudent-and-deliberate technical debt from reckless messes, and quantifying the cost of bad code to justify investment to the business rather than pursuing a big-bang rewrite, which is described as "almost always the wrong answer" [shard_04165_35514].
Finally, expect an adjustment period: smaller PRs generate more review comments per line changed, which can initially feel like more friction even though it reflects reviewers actually engaging rather than rubber-stamping, and this is the tradeoff of quality for perceived slowdown that your team should be prepared to interpret correctly [shard_06420_4716].
